question.knowledge_point: Finding the Indefinite Integral of a Exponential-Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts
question.worked_solution:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2{e}^{2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2x}(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})-\int (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})(2{e}^{2x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2}{3}\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2}{3}J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2{e}^{2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2x}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3})(2{e}^{2x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{2}{3}\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{2}{3}I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-\frac{{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2}{3}J \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2}{3}(\frac{{e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{2}{3}I) \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2{e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{9}-\frac{4}{9}I \\ \frac{13}{9}I & =\frac{2{e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-3{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{9} \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{2x}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))}{13}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Indefinite Integral of a Exponential-Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts
question.worked_solution:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{6x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6{e}^{6x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(6{e}^{6x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-6\int {e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-6J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{6x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6{e}^{6x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{6x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(6{e}^{6x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+6\int {e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+6I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-6J \\ I & ={e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-6(-{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+6I) \\ I & ={e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+6{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-36I \\ 37I & ={e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+6{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{6x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+6\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}{37}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Maclaurin Expansion of a Logarithmic Function
question.problem: Find the first three non-zero terms of the Maclaurin expansion of $\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1+x}{1-4x}).$
question.worked_solution:
First, using the laws of logarithms, we observe that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1+x}{1-4x}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+x)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-4x).\end{aligned}
$$

For the expansion of $\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+x),$ we recall the standard result

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+x) & =x-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

To obtain the expansion of $\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-4x),$ we replace $x$ with $-4x$ in the standard expansion:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-4x) & =(-4x)-\frac{(-4x)^{2}}{2}+\frac{(-4x)^{3}}{3}-⋯ \\  & =-4x-8{x}^{2}-\frac{64{x}^{3}}{3}-⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, subtracting the expansion for $\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-4x)$ from the expansion for $\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1+x}{1-4x}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+x)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-4x) \\  & =(x-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-⋯)-(-4x-8{x}^{2}-\frac{64{x}^{3}}{3}-⋯) \\  & =(1+4)x+(-\frac{1}{2}+8){x}^{2}+(\frac{1}{3}+\frac{64}{3}){x}^{3}+⋯ \\  & =5x+\frac{15{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{65{x}^{3}}{3}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Determining Whether Three Vectors are Coplanar
question.problem: Find $t$ given that the vectors $p=⟨t,1,t⟩$, $q=⟨2,-1,-1⟩$, and $r=⟨3,0,1⟩$ are coplanar.
question.worked_solution:
Computing the triple product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}p\cdot (q\times r) & =|\begin{aligned}t & 1 & t \\ 2 & -1 & -1 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =t\cdot |\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|-1\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}|+t\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =t((-1)\cdot 1-0\cdot (-1))-(2\cdot 1-3\cdot (-1))+t(2\cdot 0-3\cdot (-1)) \\  & =-t-5+3t \\  & =2t-5.\end{aligned}
$$

    

Three vectors are coplanar if and only if their triple product is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}p\cdot (q\times r) & =0 \\ 2t-5 & =0 \\ 2t & =5 \\ t & =\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the three vectors are coplanar if and only if $t=\frac{5}{2}.$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating Improper Integrals Involving Arctangent Using Substitution
question.worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u=\sqrt{x}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\,⟹\,2\,\text{d}u=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to \infty $ when $x\to \infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=\sqrt{x}$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $1$ | $\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}(x+1)}\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{u}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}(x+1)}\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{u}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}\frac{1}{{u}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(u)]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =2\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(a)-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1)] \\  & =2\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(a)]-\frac{\pi }{4})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x),$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)]=-\frac{\pi }{2}$

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)]=\frac{\pi }{2}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14052212/assets/46e6cf2950c99831a7445a862fb36a6a7b8f9233a82e49c7cf5da4a383ec4756.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}(x+1)}\,\text{d}x & =2\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(a)]-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =2\cdot (\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals of Algebraic Functions Using Substitution
question.worked_solution:
Let $u=z+4.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}z}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}z=\text{d}u.
$$

We also note that
$z+5=u+1.$

Now we can solve the integral in terms of $u,$ and then express our final answer in terms of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{z+5}{\sqrt{z+4}}\,\text{d}z & =\int \frac{u+1}{\sqrt{u}}\,\text{d}z \\  & =\int \frac{u}{\sqrt{u}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\,\text{d}z \\  & =\int \sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u+\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u+\int {u}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{2{u}^{3/2}}{3}+2\sqrt{u}+C \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{(z+4)^{3}}}{3}+2\sqrt{z+4}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals of Algebraic Functions Using Substitution
question.problem: Given that $u=x-1$, which integral is equivalent to $\int x\sqrt[5]{x-1}\,\text{d}x?$
question.worked_solution:
Since $u=x-1,$ then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

We also note that
$x=u+1.$

Now we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\sqrt[5]{x-1}\,\text{d}x & =\int (u+1)(\sqrt[5]{u})(\text{d}u) \\  & =\int (u+1)({u}^{1/5})(\text{d}u) \\  & =\int ({u}^{6/5}+{u}^{1/5})\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Approximating the Value of a Function at a  Point Using Its Taylor Series
question.problem: Use the first three non-zero terms of the Taylor expansion of $\sqrt{x}$ about $x=4$ to approximate the value of $\sqrt{\pi }.$ Give your answer to $4$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $a=4.$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\sqrt{x}={x}^{1/2} \\ f(4) & ={4}^{1/2}=2 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2} \\ {f}^{′}(4) & =\frac{1}{2}(4)^{-1/2}=\frac{1}{{2}^{2}} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{1}{2}){x}^{-3/2}=-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{-3/2} \\ {f}^{″}(4) & =-\frac{1}{4}(4)^{-3/2}=-\frac{1}{{2}^{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{x} & =2+\frac{1}{{2}^{2}}(x-4)-\frac{1}{2!}(\frac{1}{{2}^{5}})(x-4)^{2}+⋯ \\  & =2+\frac{x-4}{4}-\frac{(x-4)^{2}}{64}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=\pi $ into the above to approximate $\sqrt{\pi }.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\pi } & ≈2+\frac{\pi -4}{4}-\frac{(\pi -4)^{2}}{64} \\  & =1.773\,9\,,\end{aligned}
$$

to $4$ decimal places.

question.knowledge_point: Approximating the Value of a Function at a  Point Using Its Taylor Series
question.problem: Use the first three non-zero terms of the Taylor expansion for $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)$ about $x=0$ to approximate the value of $\operatorname{ln}⁡(1.5).$ Give your answer to $3$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $a=0.$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1) \\ f(0) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1)=0 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{x+1} \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =\frac{1}{0+1}=1 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}} \\ {f}^{″}(0) & =-\frac{1}{(0+1)^{2}}=-1 \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =\frac{2}{(x+1)^{3}} \\ {f}^{‴}(0) & =\frac{2}{(0+1)^{3}}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1) & =(0)+(1)(x-0)+\frac{(-1)}{2!}(x-0)^{2}+\frac{(2)}{3!}(x-0)^{3}+⋯ \\  & =x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=0.5$ into the above to approximate $\operatorname{ln}⁡(1.5).$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡1.5 & ≈(0.5)-\frac{1}{2}(0.5)^{2}+\frac{1}{3}(0.5)^{3} \\  & =0.417\,,\end{aligned}
$$

to three decimal places.

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Standard Matrix of a Dilation Given a Vector and its Image
question.problem: A  linear transformation $T$ represents a dilation. Given that $v=[\begin{aligned}9 \\ -5\end{aligned}]$ and $T(v)=[\begin{aligned}72 \\ -40\end{aligned}],$ what is the standard matrix of $T?$
question.worked_solution:
We can write $T(v)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(v) & =[\begin{aligned}72 \\ -40\end{aligned}] \\  & =8\cdot [\begin{aligned}9 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =8v\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $T(v)=8v,$ and so the linear transformation $T$ is a dilation with scale factor $k=8.$

The matrix that represents a dilation of scale factor $k$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}k & 0 \\ 0 & k\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the standard matrix of $T$ is

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}8 & 0 \\ 0 & 8\end{aligned}].
$$

question.problem: A linear transformation $T$ represents a dilation.  Given that $v=[\begin{aligned}-54 \\ 81\end{aligned}]$ and $T(v)=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 9\end{aligned}],$ what is the standard matrix of $T?$
question.worked_solution:
We can write $T(v)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(v) & =[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 9\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-54 \\ 81\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}v\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $T(v)=\frac{1}{9}v,$ and so the linear transformation $T$ is a dilation with scale factor $k=\frac{1}{9}.$

The matrix that represents a dilation of scale factor $k$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}k & 0 \\ 0 & k\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the standard matrix of $T$ is

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{9} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{9}\end{aligned}].
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Second-Degree Taylor Polynomial of a Given Function About a Point
question.problem: The second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+x}}$ about $x=0$ is
question.worked_solution:
To find the second-degree Taylor polynomial about $x=0,$ we plug $a=0$ into the general formula to give

$$
{P}_{2}(x)=f(0)+{f}^{′}(0)(x-0)+\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(0)(x-0)^{2}.
$$

So, we need to work out $f(0),$ ${f}^{′}(0),$ and ${f}^{″}(0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+x}}=(1+x)^{-1/2} & ⟹ &  & f(0) & =1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{1}{2}(1+x)^{-3/2} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{′}(0) & =-\frac{1}{2} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =\frac{3}{4}(1+x)^{-5/2} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{″}(0) & =\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

We now plug the results for $f(0),$ ${f}^{′}(0),$ and ${f}^{″}(0)$ into our second-degree Taylor polynomial. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(x) & =1+(-\frac{1}{2})x+(\frac{3}{4})\cdot \frac{1}{2}{x}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{3}{8}{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
